## Introduction

### N170 Component Characteristics
The polarity of the N170 ERP is negative, displaying a voltage peak at a latency of approximately 170ms post-stimulus onset (Gao et al., 2019). The most topographically active areas when the N170 is elicited are the bilateral occipito-temporal areas, specifically, electrodes P7, P8, PO7 and PO8 with a standard 10-20 system (Johnston et al., 2015; Navajas et al., 2013). 

### Background Research on the N170 Component
#### Initial Observations of the N170
The N170 was first officially observed by Bentin et al. (1996), utilising electroencephalography (EEG) to study facial perception. Bentin et al. (1996) found that visual stimuli of a human face elicited an N170 at approximately 172ms, and prominence over the posterior temporal scalp, particularly over the right hemisphere. Bentin et al. (1996) found that distorted human faces evoked the same amplitude and latency as normal human faces, while inverted human faces displayed a similar amplitude to upright human faces, albeit, a slightly delay in the N170 component. A distinct difference is that the N170 was not elicited by animal faces, human hands or inanimate objects, positing that the N170 may reflect the brain’s recognition of human faces, and specifically, eye recognition (Bentin et al., 1996).

Despite the first formal publication of the N170 from Bentin et al. (1996), Bötzel & Grüsser (1989) were the first to informally observe  findings related to facial perception through the component now known as the Vertex Positive Potential (VPP). Bötzel & Grüsser (1989) observed the VPP after providing visual stimuli of human faces amongst visual controls of chairs and trees. The VPP occurred at electrode Cz between 150ms to 200ms post-stimulus onset of the human faces. Through utilisation of a larger number of electrodes, Bötzel et al. (1995) found that the VPP was a direct three-dimensional correspondent to the N170 found at the occipito-temporal sites. Finally, Bötzel et al. (1995) undertook advanced computer analysis of dipoles, finding that the electrical signals originated deep in the temporal cortex, crossing the visual cortex and centre of the scalp. Prior to Bötzel & Grüsser’s (1989) use of EEG to understand human facial processing, researchers largely relied on animal studies and research with prosopagnosia patients (Taubert et al., 2020; Albonico & Barton, 2019). Thus, the works of Bötzel & Grüsser (1989) serve as a pivotal methodological advances in understanding the processes of human facial processing.

#### Conditions where the N170 Component is elicited
The classic visual stimuli utilised to elicit the N170 ERP component is human facial stimuli (Eimer, 2011). Inverted human faces similarly elicit the N170 component, however, with an increased amplitude and delayed deflection comparatively (Civile et al., 2018). Varying human facial expression, such as fear, have been seen to inflate the N170  amplitude (Blau et al., 2007). Human eyes are a salient visual stimuli of the N170, eliciting a greater amplitude than that of a whole human face (Bentin et al., 1996). However, visual stimuli of the nose and lips display a delay in the N170 and decrease in amplitude compared to visual stimuli of a whole human face (Bentin et al., 1996). While the N170 ERP component is particularly sensitive to facial visual stimuli, it can also be elicited by written words (Eimer, 2011; Maurer et al., 2005). 

#### Functional Significance of the N170 Component
The Face Perception Paradigm utilises EEG experimentation to evoke an N170 component (Yildirim-Keles et al., 2025). The N170 is thought to represent visual facial detection and encoding in a gestalt manner (Olivares et al., 2015). The N170 ERP is generally evoked by presenting participants with visual stimuli of faces amongst visual stimuli of objects, providing a relative ‘baseline’ between facial and non-facial visual stimuli (Rossion, 2014). Furthermore, the N170 can be applied clinically as a quantitative biomarker for autistic spectrum disorder, schizophrenia and developmental prosopagnosia, as such conditions display an uncharacteristic N170 component (Johnston et al., 2015).

Therefore, results were analysed from 37 participants. The new sample contained 24 females and 13 males, with an average age of 21.5 years and a standard deviation of 2.96 years. The age range of participants was 18 to 30 years and 35 participants were right-handed.

    "low_cutoff": 0.1,

}

#### Epoching parameters

```{python}
TMIN = -0.2 # epoch start relative to critical event
TMAX = 0.8  # epoch end relative to critical event

BASELINE = (-0.2,0) # baseline interval

# critical conditions for averaging and epoching
CONDITIONS = ["stimulus/face", "stimulus/car", "stimulus/scrambled_face", "stimulus/scrambled_car"]

REJECT = {
    "eeg": 150e-6,
    "eog": 250e-6
}

```

## Data analysis

### Preprocessing

```{python}
#| eval: true # set this to false if you don't want preprocessing to recompute
#| output: false # this suppresses any output

for raw_file in RAW_PATH.glob("*_raw.fif.gz"):

    # extract subject number
    subj_ID = raw_file.stem.split("_")[0]

    # read in raw file 
    raw = SimpleRaw(raw_file)

    # preprocess raw file
    # note how we draw on a custom preprocessing function here
    processed = preprocess(raw, 
                            reref_params = REFERENCE, 
                            filter_low_cutoff = FILTER_SETTINGS["low_cutoff"], 
                            filter_high_cutoff = FILTER_SETTINGS["high_cutoff"])
    
    processed.save(PROCESSED_PATH / f"{subj_ID}_raw.fif.gz", overwrite = True)


```

### Epoching and averaging

```{python}
#| output: false

# initialise empty dictionary to hold single-subject averages
ss_avs = {}

for cond in CONDITIONS:
    ss_avs[cond] = []

for processed_file in PROCESSED_PATH.glob("*_raw.fif.gz"):

    subj_ID = processed_file.stem.split("_")[0]
    print(f"processing participant {subj_ID}")

    if subj_ID in EXCLUDE:
        continue
    
    # read in preprocessed file
    processed = SimpleRaw(processed_file)

    # extract events
    events, event_id = processed.get_events()

    # epoch data
    epochs = SimpleEpoch(processed, events, event_id, tmin = TMIN, tmax = TMAX, baseline = BASELINE, reject = REJECT)

    # subset epochs and average by condition 
    for cond in CONDITIONS:
        av = epochs[cond].average()
        ss_avs[cond].append(av)

```

### Grand average

```{python}
#| output: false

# create an empty dict to hold our grand averages
grand_avs = {}

for cond in CONDITIONS:
    grand = grand_average(ss_avs[cond])
    grand_avs[cond] = grand
```
